title: Choosing the turban
hookLine: young Sikhs decide for themselves how to keep kesh and turban

lines: A STRIP OF CLOTH AND A TUTORIAL.
cards: Sunday morning. A teenager stands at the bathroom mirror with a long strip of cloth over one shoulder and a phone propped against the tap, playing a tying tutorial at half speed. Fold, wrap, pin, start again.
Down the hall, a younger brother still wears a patka, the small cloth their mother ties for him each morning. The teenager could have kept the patka, or stopped covering at all.
Instead, the cloth goes round once more, and this morning, it holds.

teach.h: KESH: ONE OF THE FIVE ARTICLES.
teach.b: Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles of faith. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs who have taken amrit to keep their hair uncut, and the turban covers and honors it.
Young Sikhs come to this in different ways.

teach.h: PATKA, TURBAN, KESKI, OR NOT YET.
teach.b: Some grow up in a patka and move to a full turban. Some girls choose a turban, or a keski, a smaller one. Some cut their hair for years and later grow it back.
Families argue about it, pray about it, and still sit down to dinner. The gurdwara door stays open to all of them. Why does choice matter?
Tradition remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being: he asked who would come forward, and one by one, five did.

And the Rehat Maryada asks that those who take amrit be old enough to understand what they're promising. The Khalsa begins with a person stepping forward. Today the choice can mean first tries that come out lopsided.
Ask Sikhs about a first turban and you hear kind words: looks good; practice makes perfect; nobody should judge your pagg at the gurdwara. Many start with a simpler style and grow into it.

teach.h: WORN TO SCHOOL, WORK AND THE FIELD.
teach.b: It can mean wearing a turban to a new school, a job interview or a sports field, and answering the same question politely, again and again.
It can mean waiting until you're sure. Some Sikhs put it this way: a turban tied because you chose it becomes a promise you keep.

how: Sikhs who take amrit keep kesh, uncut hair, as one of the five articles of faith, and Sikh men and some Sikh women cover it with a turban. Some young Sikhs begin with a patka and decide for themselves when to tie a full turban.

games.why: young Sikhs decide for themselves, and the tradition remembers five who stepped forward by choice. some Sikhs call a chosen turban a promise kept.

practice: Bring to mind one person who chose something you might not have chosen: what they wear, what they believe, what they gave up or took on.

Breathe in and picture them making that decision, maybe at a mirror, maybe late at night; breathe out and let go of the urge to vote on it, because it's theirs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Kesh. Uncut hair, which young Sikhs choose for themselves how to keep and whether and how to cover with a turban, a choice the tradition wants made with understanding. Today's word.
